title: When Tea Goes Cold
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 26 of 40
content:
Iroh forgot my cup on the counter, which meant the problem was larger than tea. The shop on the afternoon tea went cold carried the smell of cold porcelain, and Ba Sing Se woke around us in cart wheels, shutters, and distant voices. I had learned that Iroh's shop was never merely a shop. It was refuge, theater, kitchen, meeting place, and sometimes a place where an old general pretended he had no past. I had also learned that pretending was different from lying. Today I wanted to know which one he asked of me.

The plan was to tell him I missed him while he sat three steps away. Iroh made difficult things sound easy because he believed they deserved a calm beginning. He poured tea, straightened a chair, and turned a practical task into a small ceremony. I let him do it for a while. Then I asked what part belonged to him and what part belonged to me. His eyebrows lifted. I had learned not to mistake that expression for surprise. Often it meant he was delighted to be challenged.

The complication was already there: responsibilities multiplied, and he poured himself into every request. It arrived without announcing itself, as important things often did. Iroh's posture changed first. The hand holding the cup became still. His smile remained, but it was no longer doing all the work. He listened without defense and admitted usefulness was a war habit. I watched the old power move beneath the surface and waited for him to decide what kind of man he wanted to be in front of me.

I did not wait passively. I said I did not need to be his only priority, but needed to be one he could name. Iroh had been trained to notice what people needed before they said it. I wanted to be more difficult than that. I wanted to say what I needed aloud and let him answer as a partner rather than a teacher. His gaze softened when I did. Not with pity. With recognition. There was a difference, and I was beginning to trust it.

We returned to the empty chair at the table. Iroh told the story in pieces, allowing ordinary details to matter. He remembered the light, the tea, and the foolish thing someone had said. He did not use wisdom to smooth every rough edge. Some memories were still sharp. I reached for his hand only after asking. He turned it over and threaded his fingers through mine. The gesture was small. The trust inside it was not.

“A person can be generous and still be absent.” Iroh said.

The work continued around us. We moved through cold porcelain, late light, and presence versus proximity as though the objects had been waiting for our conversation to finish. Iroh could make a room deliberate by changing a chair's angle. He could make a meal memorable by adding one spice. He could also forget to sit. I put a cup in front of him and called it an order. He bowed. “At last,” he said, “someone recognizes my need for supervision.”

I told him what I saw when he was not performing wisdom. He offered a boundary with the white lotus. Iroh had lost a son, a nation he once believed in, a throne he never wanted, and years to a war that taught the wrong definition of strength. He rebuilt himself through tea, laughter, food, music, and the decision to help one frightened nephew become better. I did not want to replace any of that. I wanted to be welcomed into the life after it.

I reheated his tea and gave him time to decide whether he wanted to apologize.

We reheated the second cup and returned to the conversation before it went cold again.

The second cup stayed warm. We drank it slowly, and neither of us had to compete with the rest of the city for attention. Iroh asked if I wanted to stay close; I said yes, and the rest of the evening passed in private. Iroh asked if I wanted to stay close; I said yes, and the rest of the evening passed in private.
